significance: "Market-based instruments such as payments and tradable permits induce landowners to conserve habitat voluntarily. They need a single currency for habitats that differ in type, area and connectivity, and the thesis observes that most existing schemes value a site by its local quality and size alone. A site’s worth, however, also depends on its neighbours and on timing, and a land-use change on one site alters the value of nearby ones. Landowners therefore affect one another, yet have limited information about one another. An apparent remedy, in the thesis’s account, is to build spatial dependence into the market values. The problem the thesis takes on is how to design incentives without assuming that conservation value is local and static, or that ecology alone can set it. The thesis argues that incentives for market-based conservation must account for space, time and the behaviour of landowners, and that their design needs ecology and economics analysed together. In a two-species case, the ranking of conservation options under objectives that add up species’ survival probabilities can change when the time horizon (the date at which survival is judged) crosses a critical value. In a model that couples a metapopulation (a set of linked local populations) with landowners as individual agents, incentives that reward connectivity are more cost-effective than purely area-based ones, and the best design depends on how far species disperse and how costs vary in space and time. Incentive design and landowners’ social organisation strongly affect where habitat ends up and what it costs. In a simulated market for wet grasslands and reed marshes in the Netherlands, spatial incentives and a tax on habitat relocation can control the amount, fragmentation and dynamics of habitat (that paper was in preparation at submission). The thesis reads these results as showing that simple spatial and temporal incentives are a policy option for real conservation markets. It adds that the best incentives depend on the species and the economic setting, so schemes need “ecological-economic surrogates”, that is, indicators linking incentives to conservation success in a given setting. It also calls for experiments on landowner behaviour (the thesis presents a network game) and for socio-economic data, and argues that time preferences are a normative choice to be stated explicitly."

## Abstract

<p>When designing financial incentives for voluntary conservation of threatened habitats and ecosystems, we are faced with the problem that there is no single indicator for "biodiversity value". The value of a habitat depends on multiple factors such as habitat type, area, and spatial and temporal connectivity. Moreover, not only are there local trade-offs between these indicators, but land use changes at one location may also change the value of sites in the vicinity. This doctoral thesis analyzes the consequences of including trade-offs and interactions between sites in market-based conservation schemes. We ask the following questions: How can trade-offs between the survival of different species be quantified? How can spatial processes and temporal processes be included in market-based conservation, in particular the value of spatial and temporal connectivity? And how do underlying economic dynamics relate to the spatio-temporal allocation of conservation measures in market-based conservation schemes?</p>
